Book Review
Dark Fantasy

Babel

by R.F. Kuang
★★★★☆

After being burned by Katabasis's hype, Babel completely won me over with its clever silver-based magic system, a devastating slow-burn arc from idealistic student to full revolutionary, and colonialism written with real, uncomfortable precision. Info-dumps on linguistics aside, this might be the best entry point into dark academia out there.

R.F. Kuang·March 2026

In my review of the author's other book, Katabasis, I talked about how I generally try to avoid overly hyped, heavily marketed mainstream books, since I've been burned by that hype before. While I turned out to be right to be disappointed with Katabasis, I was equally wrong about Babel. This book deserves every single bit of hype surrounding it. I actually purchased both books at the same time, Babel and Katabasis together, after finally succumbing to the marketing push around both of them. And while Katabasis left me regretting caving to that hype, Babel made me genuinely glad I did. It's rare for two books from the same author, bought in the same haul, to land on such completely opposite ends of my expectations, but that's exactly what happened here.

For anyone unfamiliar with the plot, Babel follows Robin Swift, orphaned by cholera in Canton and brought to London by the mysterious Professor Lovell, who eventually enrolls him at Oxford's Royal Institute of Translation, known simply as Babel. There, alongside a small group of fellow students from different corners of the British Empire, Robin is trained to work with silver, magical bars engraved with matched word-pairs across languages that capture and weaponize the meaning lost in translation. That silver powers the Empire's entire industrial and colonial machine, and as Robin gets pulled deeper into Babel's world, he's forced to reckon with exactly what he's helping to build, and who's paying the price for it.

First, let's get into the setting. In the author's note, Kuang states that while she tries to be as historically accurate as possible and respect the cultures and history she's drawing from, this is ultimately a work of fiction, and there might be some mistakes or deviations from the real historical record. I was honestly surprised to see a disclaimer like that included at all. Do people really get that agitated over historical liberties in a work of fantasy? This is fiction, set in a world with magic silver bars, it's not meant to be a textbook. As long as the author isn't going out of her way to be disrespectful or intentionally misrepresent a culture, I think it should be completely fine to take creative liberties and deviate from the historical record where the story needs it. That said, even though I personally think the disclaimer was unnecessary, I still respect the author for including it, it shows a level of care and awareness about the subject matter she's working with, even if I don't think she needed to justify herself to that degree.

The world Kuang builds here is genuinely fascinating. It's set in 1830s Oxford, right at the dawn of the Industrial Revolution, but with one core fantastical twist, silver bars engraved with matched word-pairs from different languages, capturing the meaning that gets lost in translation, and using that lost meaning as a literal magical power source. It's such a clever, specific idea for a magic system, one that ties directly into the book's central themes rather than existing separately from them. The British Empire's entire industrial and colonial machine runs on this silver, which means the empire is, quite literally, powered by extracted language and stolen culture, mined from the colonized world and funneled back through institutions like Babel, the Royal Institute of Translation, at the heart of Oxford. It's an incredibly elegant way to make the abstract violence of colonialism something concrete and visible on the page, since here, exploitation isn't just a background historical fact, it's the actual mechanism the entire magic system runs on.

The colonialism and sexism of this era are written so beautifully and realistically. That distinctly English, subtle brand of racism, the kind delivered with perfect manners, dressed up in politeness and academic language, rather than shouted outright, is incredibly well-crafted throughout the book. It's not the cartoonish, overtly hostile racism you sometimes see in fiction, it's the quieter, more insidious kind, backhanded compliments, condescending curiosity, the constant reminder that no matter how brilliant or accomplished you are, you'll always be treated as an outsider allowed in on sufferance rather than as an equal. Kuang captures that dynamic with real precision, the way prejudice can hide behind civility, behind academic prestige, behind the language of progress and enlightenment itself. It makes the injustice feel more insidious somehow, because it's never loud enough to easily point at and call out, yet it's everywhere, shaping every interaction Robin and his friends have with the world around them.

The main character, Robin, is so well written too. We watch him evolve from an idealistic student, someone who genuinely believes in the promise of Oxford, in the value of translation as a noble pursuit, in the idea that his own talent and hard work might actually earn him a place at the table, into someone who slowly starts questioning colonialism itself and, more painfully, his own complicity in keeping that system running. Every book he translates, every silver bar he helps craft, is directly fueling the same empire that's exploiting the country he came from, and watching that realization creep in on him, gradually rather than all at once, is genuinely one of the strongest character arcs I've read in a long time. By the end, he's transformed into someone willing to go fully revolutionary, and the book earns that transformation completely, it never feels rushed or forced, every step of his radicalization is built carefully on the step before it. It's such a great character arc, watching someone move from naive faith in a broken system to a full, clear-eyed rejection of it, without ever feeling like the story is cheating to get him there.

The side characters are also wonderfully diverse and well written. Each of them comes at the story's central themes of racism and colonialism from a genuinely different angle, so instead of getting one single perspective on what it means to exist inside this system, we get several, each shaped by different backgrounds, different countries of origin, different ways the empire has touched or exploited their lives. Some are more willing to compromise, some are far more radicalized from the start, and some sit somewhere uncomfortably in between, and that spread makes the world feel so much richer and more honest than if everyone reacted to injustice in exactly the same way. Together, they form a genuinely true friend group too, one that feels lived-in and real, full of inside jokes, quiet loyalty, and real affection between them, even as the weight of what they're all wrapped up in slowly starts to strain those bonds. Watching that friendship both sustain them and eventually fracture under the pressure of everything happening around them is one of the most emotionally effective parts of the whole book.

On the prose itself, Kuang writes with a real academic elegance, dense at times, but purposeful, her sentences carry the weight of someone who clearly knows the subject matter inside and out. It fits the dark academia tone perfectly, formal and precise during the Oxford scenes, but it also knows how to loosen up and hit hard emotionally when the story calls for it. It never feels showy for its own sake outside of the linguistics tangents, the prose itself always serves the story.

The magic system, on the other hand, felt complicated to me, and honestly too far-fetched and overly intricate at points, almost like it becomes a way for the author to flex how much linguistic knowledge she actually has rather than serving the story efficiently. This feels like a recurring problem in other books I've read from this author, I get the sense she's trying a bit too hard to convince the reader just how smart and well-researched she is, and it shows in how some chapters stretch on far longer than they need to, packed with info dumps about etymology and translation theory that I don't necessarily want or need from a fantasy novel. If I wanted a deep academic lecture on how languages actually work and evolve, I would have just bought a nonfiction book about linguistics instead. That said, to be fair to the book, the magic system does fit the story well overall, since this is a dark academia novel at its core, so having the magic be rooted in scholarship, translation, and linguistic theory makes thematic sense even when it occasionally overstays its welcome on the page.

The story's pacing goes perfectly, I have to say. Kuang does a great job balancing the slower, more contemplative academic sections with the moments where the plot actually accelerates, and the transition never feels jarring or mismatched, even as the tone of the book shifts dramatically over the course of the story. The way the story moves from a fairly grounded, coming-of-age academic setting, all lectures, exams, and the day-to-day rhythm of student life, into a full-blown revolution was genuinely amazing to watch unfold. It never feels like a sudden gear shift either, the escalation is gradual and deliberate, built scene by scene, so that by the time things boil over into open rebellion, it feels like the only possible outcome rather than some abrupt twist tacked on for drama. That slow-burn structure, patient at first, then relentless once it gets going, is honestly one of the book's greatest strengths.

I'm trying to stay spoiler-free here, but I have to say the twists, revelations, and betrayals throughout the book hit absolutely perfectly. Kuang has a real talent for planting details early on that seem completely innocuous in the moment, only for them to come crashing back with devastating weight later in the story. Nothing here feels cheap or manipulative either, every twist is earned, built on character motivations that have been carefully established from the very beginning, so even when something genuinely shocks you, looking back you can trace exactly how it was set up all along. The betrayals in particular land with real emotional force, because by that point in the book you've spent so much time with these characters, growing attached to their friendships and their shared struggles, that watching those relationships fracture under the weight of ideology and survival genuinely hurts to read. And without spoiling anything about how it actually ends, I'll just say the conclusion lands with exactly the weight it should, it's not a comfortable ending, and it isn't supposed to be.

Compared to Katabasis, what really sets Babel apart for me is how earned everything feels. Katabasis leaned hard on the author's cleverness and academic background without always translating that into something I actually cared about emotionally, it felt more interested in being impressive than in making me feel anything. Babel has that same intellectual ambition, but it's grounded in a character and a friend group I genuinely invested in, so even when the book indulges in its linguistics tangents, there's still real emotional stakes underneath holding it all together. That's the difference between a book that just wants to prove how smart its author is and one that actually uses that intelligence in service of a story worth telling.

Overall, this is a genuinely great dark academia book, and if you've never read anything in this genre before and are looking for a place to start, this might honestly be one of the best possible introductions to it. It has everything the genre promises, the atmosphere, the moral complexity, the slow descent from idealism into something much darker, wrapped around a magic system and setting that gives it a real identity of its own rather than just borrowing the aesthetic. It does suffer at points from heavier info-dumping on linguistics than the story strictly needs, and there were chapters where I felt the author was more interested in showing off her academic knowledge than moving the plot forward efficiently. But even with that flaw, this is still an overall enjoyable and well-written read, one with real emotional weight, a genuinely earned character arc, and a friend group whose bond and eventual fracture stuck with me long after finishing.

4 out of 5 stars.

By Ruşen M. Özoruç
